a: to minister to him,
t: "To minister to him": missing in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks "to minister to him" and has "to bless" for "to love" (see the next variant).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b; the Greek
readings.en: to minister to him
readings.plain: to minister to him,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The Masoretic Text is supported by the second Isaiah scroll from Cave 1 (1QIsa-b) and by the Greek. The Great Isaiah Scroll often smooths and changes words, and here it may avoid the bold claim that foreigners "minister" like priests. This entry goes with the next one on the same verse.

a: to love the name of the LORD
t: To love, or to bless, the LORD's name?
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "to bless the name of the LORD", after "to be his servants".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; 1QIsa-b; the Greek (agapan, 'to love')
readings.en: and to love the name of the LORD
readings.plain: to love the name of the LORD

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), which puts it after 'to be his servants'
readings.en: and to bless the name of the LORD
readings.plain: to bless the name of the LORD

why: The other witnesses agree on "to love". The scroll's order is "to be his servants and to bless the name of the LORD and keeping the Sabbath", a smoother list. This entry goes with the previous one.
b: The Greek also adds "male and female slaves" after "servants".

a: They lie dreaming
t: Dreaming, or seers?
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "they are seers", a different word that sounds almost the same.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 1QIsa-b
readings.en: dreaming, raving (hozim)
readings.plain: They lie dreaming

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: they are seers (chozim)
readings.plain: They are seers who lie

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: dreaming of bed
readings.plain: They dream of bed

why: Hozim occurs only here, and its meaning, "dreaming" or "panting", is guessed from Arabic and from the Greek. The scroll's "seers" is a familiar word and so probably an easier substitute; but it fits the charge that the watchmen are the people's prophets, and some scholars prefer it.

a: "Come, let me get wine,
t: A verse the Greek lacks
p: The Greek translation has no 56:12. The Hebrew and the scrolls have it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); 1QIsa-b
readings.en: Come, let me take wine
readings.plain: "Come, let me get wine,

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus; Ziegler's critical text)
readings.en: (56:12 is missing)

why: Both Cave 1 scrolls have the verse, so it was part of the Hebrew book by the 100s BC. The Greek translator of Isaiah often shortens; he may have dropped a verse he found coarse or hard.

a: 'Peace, peace,
t: "Peace, peace" or "Peace"?
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll has "peace" once; the Greek, "peace upon peace".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QIsa-d (4Q58), as preserved
readings.en: peace, peace
readings.plain: 'Peace, peace,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: peace
readings.plain: 'Peace,

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: peace upon peace
readings.plain: 'Peace upon peace,

why: The doubled word is a Hebrew way of stressing it (compare 26:3, "in peace, peace", meaning perfect peace). A copyist could easily drop one of two identical words, as the Great Isaiah Scroll seems to have done. Ephesians 2:17 has "peace" twice, matching the Hebrew.

a: if you offer your own self to the hungry
t: "Your self" or "your bread"?
p: The Greek reads "give your bread from your soul to the hungry", an easier sense.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); 1QIsa-b
readings.en: and you offer your self (nefesh) to the hungry
readings.plain: if you offer your own self to the hungry

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus)
readings.orig: καὶ δῷς πεινῶντι τὸν ἄρτον ἐκ ψυχῆς σου
readings.en: and you give bread to the hungry from your soul
readings.plain: if you give the hungry bread from your heart

why: Both Cave 1 scrolls agree with the Masoretic Text. The Greek seems to explain the bold Hebrew, adding "bread" from 58:7. The Hebrew's wordplay on nefesh (see the note) is lost in the Greek.

a: then the LORD will be your delight
t: Delight in the LORD, or trust in him?
p: The Greek has "you will trust in the Lord".

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); 1QIsa-b
readings.en: then you will delight yourself in the LORD
readings.plain: then the LORD will be your delight

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus)
readings.en: and you will be trusting in the Lord
readings.plain: then you will trust in the LORD

why: The Hebrew repeats the root of 'oneg, "delight", from 58:13: call the Sabbath a delight, and the LORD himself will be your delight. The Greek misses the link.

a: "A redeemer will come to Zion,
t: To Zion, for Zion, or from Zion?
p: The Hebrew says the redeemer comes "to Zion"; the Greek, "for the sake of Zion"; Paul, "out of Zion" (Romans 11:26).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, 'el Tsiyyon, 'to Zion')
readings.en: and a redeemer will come to Zion
readings.plain: "A redeemer will come to Zion,

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus; Ziegler's critical text)
readings.orig: καὶ ἥξει ἕνεκεν Σιὼν ὁ ῥυόμενος
readings.en: and the deliverer will come for the sake of Zion
readings.plain: "The deliverer will come for Zion's sake,

readings.w: Romans 11:26 (Paul's quotation)
readings.en: the deliverer will come out of Zion
readings.plain: "The deliverer will come out of Zion,

why: The Hebrew witnesses agree on "to Zion". The Greek translated the preposition loosely, and Paul's "out of Zion" probably blends the line with Psalm 14:7 ("Who will send Israel's rescue out of Zion?") or reflects a Greek text that had it. The next line differs too: the Hebrew says the redeemer comes "to those in Jacob who turn from rebellion", while the Greek and Paul say "he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob".
b: The difference matters to the meaning. In the Hebrew, those who repent receive the redeemer. In the Greek and in Romans 11:26, the redeemer himself takes away the sin, which is Paul's point about God's mercy to Israel.

a: to those in Jacob who turn from rebellion,"
t: Those who turn, or he who turns away?
p: The Greek and Romans 11:26 have "he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob". This entry goes with the one before.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: and to those who turn from rebellion in Jacob
readings.plain: to those in Jacob who turn from rebellion,"

readings.w: Greek (Swete's Codex Vaticanus); quoted in Romans 11:26
readings.en: and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob
readings.plain: and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob,"

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Greek seems to have read the verb as active ("he will turn back") and made rebellion its object.

a: nor will the moon give you brightness with its glow
t: "By night"
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek add "by night", to match "by day" in the line before.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and for brightness the moon will not give light to you
readings.plain: nor will the moon give you brightness with its glow

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, ballaylah 'by night'); Greek (Swete: 'the rising of the moon will not light your night'); Targum
readings.orig: ולנוגה הירח בלילה לוא יאיר לך
readings.en: and for brightness the moon by night will not give light to you
readings.plain: nor will the moon give you brightness by night

why: The longer reading balances "by day" neatly, and several modern versions adopt it. But a balanced line is exactly what a scribe or translator would create, and the shorter Hebrew makes good sense. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text and shows the scroll's reading here.

a: They are the sprout of my planting
t: My planting, his planting, the LORD's planting
p: The written Hebrew says "his planting"; the reading tradition, "my planting"; the Great Isaiah Scroll, "the LORD's planting".

readings.w: Qere, the reading tradition of the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex margin)
readings.en: the sprout of my planting
readings.plain: They are the sprout of my planting

readings.w: Ketiv, the written text of the Leningrad Codex; 1QIsa-b (1Q8), 'his plantings, the work of his hands'
readings.en: the sprout of his planting
readings.plain: They are the sprout of his planting

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), with 'the work of his hands'
readings.en: the sprout of the planting of the LORD
readings.plain: They are the sprout of the LORD's planting

why: "My planting" fits "the work of my hands" in the same line and God's speech in the context. The Ketiv "his", 1QIsa-b's "his plantings... his hands" and the Great Isaiah Scroll's "the LORD's" may come from 61:3, "the LORD's planting". The Greek has "guarding the planting, the works of his hands".

a: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me
t: "Lord GOD" or "the LORD"
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek have "the Spirit of the LORD", without "Lord" (Adonai). So does Luke 4:18.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q56 (4QIsa-b)
readings.en: the Spirit of the Lord YHWH is on me
readings.plain: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on me

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); Greek (Swete: 'Spirit of the Lord upon me'); Luke 4:18
readings.en: the Spirit of YHWH is on me
readings.plain: The Spirit of the LORD is on me

readings.w: 1Q8 (1QIsa-b), which has 'God' (Elohim) before 'on me', where the Masoretic Text has YHWH; the words before it are lost
readings.en: [the Spirit of ...] God is on me
readings.plain: The Spirit of God is on me

why: Scribes often added or dropped Adonai before the divine name, and both forms occur in Isaiah. The shorter reading of the scroll, the Greek and Luke may be older. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which 4Q56 supports.

a: and an opening wide for those who are bound
t: Opening for prisoners, or sight for the blind
p: The Greek reads "and recovery of sight to the blind", and Luke 4:18 follows it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, as one word); 4Q56
readings.en: and to the bound, an opening wide
readings.plain: and an opening wide for those who are bound

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'and sight to the blind'); Luke 4:18
readings.en: and to the blind, recovery of sight
readings.plain: and recovery of sight to the blind

why: The Greek is an interpretation of an unusual Hebrew phrase, since paqach elsewhere means opening the eyes (42:7). All the Hebrew witnesses agree on the prisoners. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the Greek reading matters because it is the one Jesus reads in Luke.

a: I hate robbery done with crookedness
t: With crookedness, or with a burnt offering
p: The Masoretic word be'olah can mean "with injustice" or "with a burnt offering". Most versions read the first, the Talmud and KJV the second.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), 'olah read as 'awlah 'injustice' (as in Job 5:16; Psalm 92:15); Greek (Swete: 'robberies from injustice'); Targum ('lying and violence')
readings.en: robbery with injustice
readings.plain: I hate robbery done with crookedness

readings.w: Masoretic Text, 'olah read as 'burnt offering'; Latin Vulgate ('rapinam in holocausto'); Bavli Sukkah 30a; KJV
readings.en: robbery in a burnt offering
readings.plain: I hate robbery done with a burnt offering

why: Both readings follow the same Masoretic text; they differ in how the word is understood. 'Olah is a known spelling of 'awlah, "injustice" (Job 5:16; Psalm 92:15), and the Greek, the Targum and the parallel with "justice" favor it. The Plain follows that sense. The Vulgate, the Talmud and the KJV ("robbery for burnt offering") take the word as "burnt offering".

a: like a bridegroom who wears his garland like a priest
t: "Acts as priest" or "like a priest"
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads kkwhn, "like a priest", where the Masoretic Text has a verb, "he acts as priest".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: like a bridegroom, he priests a headdress
readings.plain: like a bridegroom who wears his garland like a priest

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: like a bridegroom, like a priest, a headdress
readings.plain: like a bridegroom, like a priest, with his garland

why: Both readings make the same comparison. The rare verb of the Masoretic Text is the harder reading, and the scroll's simpler "like a priest" may smooth it. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: your sons will take you as wife
t: Your sons, or your builder
p: The Masoretic vowels give "your sons". With other vowels the same letters read "your builder".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); Greek (Swete: 'so your sons will dwell'); Targum
readings.en: your sons will marry you
readings.plain: your sons will take you as wife

readings.w: Revocalized as bonayikh, 'your Builder' (a plural of majesty, like 'your husband, your maker' in 54:5), a modern conjecture
readings.en: your Builder will marry you
readings.plain: your builder will take you as wife

why: Every ancient witness has "your sons", read as Zion's children settling the land again. "Your builder" gives a smoother parallel with God the bridegroom and recalls 54:5 ("For your husband is your Maker"), but it rests only on changed vowels. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: in my holy courts."
t: "Says your God"
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll adds "says your God" at the end of the oath.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 1Q8 (1QIsa-b); Greek
readings.en: in my holy courts
readings.plain: in my holy courts."

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: in my holy courts, says your God
readings.plain: in my holy courts," says your God.

why: The scroll often adds speech formulas like this one (compare 40:1, 25). The shorter text, supported by 1QIsa-b and the Greek, is likely older. The scroll also reads "the name of the LORD" for "the LORD".

a: Lift a flag over the peoples!
t: A flag, or a stumbling stone
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll ends: "clear away the stone of stumbling; say among the peoples".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 1Q8 (1QIsa-b); Greek (Swete: 'lift up a signal for the nations')
readings.en: lift a banner over the peoples
readings.plain: Lift a flag over the peoples!

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), after 'clear away the stumbling stone'
readings.en: say among the peoples
readings.plain: Say among the peoples!

why: The scroll's "stone of stumbling" comes from 57:14 and 8:14, and "say among the peoples" may lead into 62:11. The scroll also has "go through" only once. The Masoretic reading is supported by 1QIsa-b and the Greek and matches 49:22.

a: from the peoples there was no one with me
t: From the peoples, or from my people
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "from my people" instead of "from the peoples".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek ('of the nations')
readings.en: and from the peoples there was no one with me
readings.plain: from the peoples there was no one with me

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: and from my people there was no one with me
readings.plain: from my people there was no one with me

why: "My people" makes the lonely warrior's point sharper, but the other witnesses read "the peoples", who are also the grapes trodden in the next lines (63:6). The scroll's form may be a simple spelling slip.

a: I stamped on them in my anger
t: Lines skipped in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll skips from "no one with me" to "I stained everything I wore", dropping three lines. Each line has its own entry.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek
readings.en: and I trod them in my anger
readings.plain: I stamped on them in my anger

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), which lacks 'I stamped on them... on my clothes'
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The scribe's eye probably jumped between two similar line endings, a common copying error (haplography). The missing lines are in the other witnesses and are needed for the sense.

a: and crushed them underfoot in my fury.
t: Lines skipped in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll skips from "no one with me" to "I stained everything I wore", dropping three lines. Each line has its own entry.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek
readings.en: and I trampled them in my fury
readings.plain: and crushed them underfoot in my fury.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), which lacks 'I stamped on them... on my clothes'
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The scribe's eye probably jumped between two similar line endings, a common copying error (haplography). The missing lines are in the other witnesses and are needed for the sense.

a: Their juice spattered on my clothes,
t: Lines skipped in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll skips from "no one with me" to "I stained everything I wore", dropping three lines. Each line has its own entry.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek
readings.en: and their juice spattered on my clothes
readings.plain: Their juice spattered on my clothes,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), which lacks 'I stamped on them... on my clothes'
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The scribe's eye probably jumped between two similar line endings, a common copying error (haplography). The missing lines are in the other witnesses and are needed for the sense.

a: I made them drunk in my fury
t: Made them drunk, or shattered them
p: Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Targum read "I shattered them", differing by one letter.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: and I made them drunk in my fury
readings.plain: I made them drunk in my fury

readings.w: Some medieval Hebrew manuscripts; Targum
readings.en: and I shattered them in my fury
readings.plain: I shattered them in my fury

why: The Hebrew letters kaf and bet look alike. "Made them drunk" fits the wine imagery and the cup of fury in 51:17–23, and it is the reading of the oldest witness, the scroll. "Shattered" fits "stamped down". The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: In every trouble of theirs, trouble came to him
t: Ketiv "not", Qere "to him"
p: The written text has lo' "not", which the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Greek support; the reading tradition has lo "to him".

readings.w: Qere, the reading tradition of the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex margin); Targum
readings.en: in all their distress, to him there was distress
readings.plain: In every trouble of theirs, trouble came to him

readings.w: Ketiv, the written text of the Leningrad Codex; Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, spelled lw')
readings.en: in all their distress, he did not distress (them)
readings.plain: In every trouble of theirs, he did not afflict them

readings.w: Greek (Swete), joining 'not' to the next line
readings.orig: ἐκ πάσης θλίψεως αὐτῶν. οὐ πρέσβυς οὐδὲ ἄγγελος, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸς ἔσωσεν αὐτούς
readings.en: out of all their affliction. Not an envoy nor an angel, but he himself saved them
readings.plain: from every trouble of theirs. No envoy and no angel, but he himself saved them

why: The written consonants have "not", and the Greek shows how early that was read. But the reading tradition makes better sense of the Hebrew line as it stands, and it gives the verse its famous meaning, that God suffers with his people. The Plain follows the Qere, and notes the written form here.

a: with the shepherds of his flock
t: Shepherds or shepherd
p: The Greek, the Targum and some Hebrew manuscripts have the singular, "the shepherd of his flock", meaning Moses.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: with the shepherds of his flock
readings.plain: with the shepherds of his flock

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'the shepherd of the sheep'); Targum; some medieval Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: the shepherd of the sheep
readings.plain: with the shepherd of his flock

why: The plural and singular differ only in a vowel letter. The plural fits Psalm 77:20 (Moses and Aaron), and is the reading of the scroll. The singular makes the line about Moses alone, who is named just before.

a: When you did fearsome things we did not hope for
t: Things we did not hope for
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks "not": "fearsome things we hoped for". The Greek lacks the middle of the verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: when you did fearsome things we did not hope for
readings.plain: When you did fearsome things we did not hope for

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: when you did fearsome things we hoped for
readings.plain: When you did fearsome things we hoped for

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'when you do glorious things, trembling will take hold of the mountains')
readings.en: when you do glorious things
readings.plain: When you do glorious things

why: "Things we did not hope for" means wonders beyond expectation, like those at the exodus. The scroll's reading may have lost a short word. The Greek joins the verse's end to its start and drops "we did not hope for, you came down", which repeats 64:1.

a: We have stayed in them a long time. Will we be saved?
t: An uncertain line
p: The Greek reads "therefore we went astray". The Hebrew is hard, and scholars have corrected it in many ways.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: in them a long time, and shall we be saved?
readings.plain: We have stayed in them a long time. Will we be saved?

readings.w: Greek (Swete)
readings.en: therefore we went astray
readings.plain: Because of this we went astray.

why: The Hebrew and the scroll agree, so the difficulty is old. The Greek translator may have read a different text or guessed. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and reads the last word as a question.

a: and let us melt away in the grip of our wrongdoing
t: Melted us, or handed us over
p: The Greek, the Targum and the Syriac read "you handed us over" because of our sins.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), vattemugenu
readings.en: and you made us melt by the hand of our wrongdoing
readings.plain: and let us melt away in the grip of our wrongdoing

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'you handed us over because of our sins'); Targum; Syriac; perhaps the Great Isaiah Scroll's wtmgdnw, read as vattemaggenenu
readings.orig: καὶ παρέδωκας ἡμᾶς διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν
readings.en: and you handed us over because of our sins
readings.plain: and handed us over to the power of our wrongdoing

why: The two readings differ by one letter (mug, "melt", and miggen, "hand over", as in Genesis 14:20). "Handed us over into the hand of" is a common biblical phrase, and many scholars prefer it. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: to a nation that was not called by my name
t: Not called by my name, or did not call on my name
p: The Masoretic vowels read "was not called by my name". The Greek and other versions read "did not call on my name".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), vocalized qora'
readings.en: to a nation that was not called by my name
readings.plain: to a nation that was not called by my name

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'which did not call my name'); Targum; Syriac; Latin; read as qara'
readings.orig: τῷ ἔθνει οἳ οὐκ ἐκάλεσάν μου τὸ ὄνομα
readings.en: to a nation that did not call on my name
readings.plain: to a nation that did not call on my name

why: The consonants allow both. The Masoretic reading echoes 63:19, "like those who were not called by your name", and can point to foreigners, as Paul read it. The other reading matches 64:7, "No one calls on your name", and points to Israel. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: and making smoke on the bricks,
t: Bricks, or stones
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads something like "and they suck hands on the stones". The Greek adds "to demons, which do not exist".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and making smoke on the bricks
readings.plain: and making smoke on the bricks,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: and they suck (?) hands on the stones
readings.plain: and they suck hands on the stones,

readings.w: Greek (Swete)
readings.orig: καὶ θυμιῶσιν ἐπὶ ταῖς πλίνθοις τοῖς δαιμονίοις ἃ οὐκ ἔστιν
readings.en: and burn incense on the bricks to demons, which do not exist
readings.plain: and making smoke on the bricks to demons that do not exist,

why: The scroll's reading is obscure. Some scholars see a rite of kissing or sucking the hand, or a misreading of the Hebrew, perhaps reading yanqu "suck" for a form of "empty out" or "pour". The Greek adds an explanation. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: with broth of foul meat in their pots
t: Broth or pieces
p: The written Hebrew has "pieces" (peraq); the reading tradition, "broth" (meraq). The Great Isaiah Scroll has "broth".

readings.w: Qere, the reading tradition (Leningrad Codex margin); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); Greek ('broth of sacrifices')
readings.en: and broth of foul things in their vessels
readings.plain: with broth of foul meat in their pots

readings.w: Ketiv, the written text of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: and pieces of foul things in their vessels
readings.plain: with pieces of foul meat in their pots

why: Mem and pe are not easily confused, but both words make sense. The reading tradition is supported by the scroll and the Greek. Piggul is sacrificial meat left too long, which the law calls "foul" (Leviticus 7:18; Leviticus 19:7).

a: Do not come near me
t: Come near, or touch
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "do not touch me" for "do not come near me".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek ('do not come near me')
readings.en: do not come near me
readings.plain: Do not come near me

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: do not touch me
readings.plain: Do not touch me

why: The verbs look alike in Hebrew (tiggash and tigga'). "Touch" fits the idea of holiness passed on by contact, but the Masoretic reading is supported by the Greek. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: But his servants he will call by another name,
t: A line missing in the Great Isaiah Scroll
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll ends the curse with "forever" and lacks the line about another name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek ('those who serve me will be called by a new name')
readings.en: and his servants he will call by another name
readings.plain: But his servants he will call by another name,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), which reads 'So may the Lord GOD kill you forever' and lacks this line
readings.en: (no words here)

why: The scroll may have dropped the line by accident or changed it. The promise of a new name is in the Masoretic Text and the Greek, and fits 62:2. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: will ask it by the God of Amen
t: The God of Amen, or the true God
p: The Greek translates "Amen" as "true": "the true God". The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the verse's first clause.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Latin Vulgate ('in Deo amen')
readings.en: by the God of Amen
readings.plain: will ask it by the God of Amen

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'the true God')
readings.en: the true God
readings.plain: will ask it by the true God

why: The Greek translates the meaning of the word; it does not point to a different Hebrew text, and the Vulgate keeps "amen". The Plain keeps the Hebrew word because Revelation 3:14 takes it up as a name. The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the first clause ("whoever asks for a blessing in the land will ask it by the God of Amen") and instead reads "And it will be: whoever swears by the God of Amen, and whoever swears in the land will swear by the God of Amen". Where the scroll has this line, it too reads "the God of Amen".

a: For like the lifetime of a tree
t: A tree, or the tree of life
p: The Greek and the Targum read "like the days of the tree of life".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: for like the days of the tree
readings.plain: For like the lifetime of a tree

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'according to the days of the tree of life'); Targum
readings.orig: κατὰ γὰρ τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς
readings.en: for according to the days of the tree of life
readings.plain: For like the lifetime of the tree of life

why: The Greek and Targum add an interpretation that links the verse to Eden (Genesis 2:9; Genesis 3:22). The Hebrew witnesses agree on "the tree", meaning a long-lived tree. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: One who slaughters an ox, one who kills a man;
t: Joined, or compared
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "like one who strikes a man", making a comparison. The Greek uses "as" through the verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: one who slaughters the ox, one who strikes a man
readings.plain: One who slaughters an ox, one who kills a man;

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: one who slaughters the ox is like one who strikes a man
readings.plain: One who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man;

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'the lawless one who sacrifices a calf to me is as one who kills a dog')
readings.orig: ὁ θύων μοι μόσχον ὡς ἀποκτέννων κύνα
readings.en: one who sacrifices a calf to me, as one killing a dog
readings.plain: One who sacrifices an ox to me is like one who kills a dog;

why: The scroll and the Greek both read the pairs as comparisons, as most translations do. The Masoretic Text, without "like", is the harder reading and also allows the sense of people who do both. The Plain follows it and leaves the pairing bare.

a: so we can see your joy!'
t: We will see, or he will appear
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "he will appear" (yera'eh) for "we will see" (nir'eh).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: and we will see your joy
readings.plain: so we can see your joy!'

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a); Greek ('that it may be seen in their joy')
readings.en: he will appear in your joy
readings.plain: he will appear in your joy!'

why: The words differ by one letter. The scroll's reading turns the mockery into a promise ("he will appear to your joy"), which the KJV also gives. The Masoretic Text keeps the mockers' taunt. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.

a: For by fire the LORD will judge
t: Will judge, or will come to judge
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "For by fire the LORD will come to judge".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Greek
readings.en: for by fire the LORD will enter into judgment
readings.plain: For by fire the LORD will judge

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: for by fire the LORD will come to judge
readings.plain: For by fire the LORD will come to judge

why: The scroll's wording repeats "will come" from 66:15 and smooths the rare form nishpat. The Masoretic Text is supported by the Greek.

a: following one in the middle
t: Qere "one" (feminine), Ketiv "one" (masculine)
p: The written Hebrew has masculine 'echad, the reading tradition feminine 'achat; English "one" covers both. The Greek has "in the porches".

readings.w: Qere, the reading tradition (Leningrad Codex margin); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: after one (feminine) in the middle
readings.plain: following one in the middle

readings.w: Ketiv, the written text of the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: after one (masculine) in the middle
readings.plain: following one in the middle

readings.w: Greek (Swete: 'and in the porches eating')
readings.en: and in the porches
readings.plain: and in the gateways

why: English "one" fits both forms, so the Plain reads the same either way; it follows the Qere, as elsewhere in this part. The masculine may mean a leader of the rite; the feminine has been taken as a priestess or goddess, or as an adverb ("one after another"). The Great Isaiah Scroll also lacks "will come to an end" and reads "says the LORD", leaving the verse with no main verb.

a: to Tarshish, Pul and Lud, who draw the bow
t: Pul or Put; bow-drawers or Meshech
p: The Greek reads Phoud (Put) for Pul and Mosoch (Meshech) for "who draw the bow".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) has 'Tarshish, Pul and Lud' (the next words are lost)
readings.en: Tarshish, Pul and Lud, drawers of the bow
readings.plain: to Tarshish, Pul and Lud, who draw the bow

readings.w: Greek (Swete)
readings.orig: εἰς Θαρσεὶς καὶ Φοὺδ καὶ Λοὺδ καὶ Μόσοχ
readings.en: to Tharsis and Phoud and Loud and Mosoch
readings.plain: to Tarshish, Put, Lud and Meshech

why: Pul and Put differ in one letter, and Put appears with Lud in Jeremiah 46:9 and Ezekiel 27:10. Moshkhe, "drawers of", has the same letters as Meshech. Many scholars think the Greek preserves the original list; the Plain follows the Hebrew. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "signs" for "a sign".

a: to be Levite priests
t: Levite priests, or priests and Levites
p: The Hebrew has "for priests, for Levites" without "and". The Greek reads "priests and Levites".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), read as one title, as in Deuteronomy
readings.en: to be priests, to be Levites
readings.plain: to be Levite priests

readings.w: Greek (Swete); many Hebrew manuscripts with 'and'
readings.en: priests and Levites
readings.plain: to be priests and Levites

why: Deuteronomy speaks of "the Levite priests" as one group (Deuteronomy 17:9; Deuteronomy 18:1), and the Hebrew without "and" fits that phrase. The Greek and some manuscripts reflect the later two-tier temple staff of priests and Levites. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds "for me".

a: all flesh will come to bow down before me,
t: "In Jerusalem"
p: The Greek adds "in Jerusalem" after "before me".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
readings.en: all flesh will come to bow down before me
readings.plain: all flesh will come to bow down before me,

readings.w: Greek (Swete)
readings.orig: ἥξει πᾶσα σὰρξ τοῦ προσκυνῆσαι ἐνώπιον ἐμοῦ ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: all flesh will come to worship before me in Jerusalem
readings.plain: all flesh will come to bow down before me in Jerusalem,

why: The Greek makes explicit what the context implies (66:20). The Hebrew witnesses agree on the shorter text.
